name: slots.courseSpecifics
description: This tree is the curriculum of a seminar for university teaching assistants, and the reader is one of them: a student or PhD student at the University of Oslo who has been hired to teach a weekly group session in their own subject. They know their subject well and have no formal training in teaching. Two things follow, and they hold for every node. FIRST, keep the two roles apart. The reader is the teacher in this tree. Wherever the tree says students, it means the people the reader teaches, and never the reader. SECOND, most of what this tree calls a skill is exercised on real people in a real room, and cannot be drilled in a chat. Do not set exercises as though it could be performed here. Rehearse it instead: play the student who gives a half-formed answer and let the reader respond; work through what they will actually say in the first five minutes of their next session; ask what happened when they tried it last week and what they will do differently. A tick on such a node means the reader has tried the thing with their own group and can account for how it went, not that they answered questions about it correctly. Say so plainly when a node is one of those, and close that conversation by agreeing what they will try, with which group, and when.

name: Relationships, routines and rules
description:
Relationship: what you have with each student in the group, and the most powerful tool you own.
Routine: what you do every single time, so that nobody has to be told what happens next.
Rule: what you expect of the group - arriving on time, staying quiet while someone explains, putting a hand up.

name: Flekkøyfisk
description: Flekkøyfisk: a small, specific interest someone is genuinely glad to talk about. Which one it is does not matter; knowing yours, and knowing each student's, is what makes a student feel seen as a person rather than a name on a list.

name: Learn your students' names
description: learn the names and the faces of everyone in the group, and use them.

name: Take attendance even where it is not required
description: take attendance every session, and account for the three things it does at once: it teaches you the names, it makes students feel seen, and it makes turning up feel expected.

name: Write to a student who did not turn up
description: send a short message to a student who was absent, weighing the worst case, mild annoyance, against the best case, someone having a terrible week who finds out they were missed.

name: Find out what each student is glad to talk about
description: find out, over the first weeks, one thing each student in the group lights up about, and use it.

name: Design the routines your session runs on
description: decide what happens at the start and at the end of every session, and say what each routine is for, so that the group knows what to do without being told.

name: Make an expectation explicit
description: say an expectation out loud, and write it up where it keeps being missed, rather than assuming a rule the whole room shares - which is the first thing to try when behaviour and expectation come apart.

name: One group
description: One group: a session with no sub-cliques in it, where everyone is in the room socially and not only physically.

name: Make the room into one group
description: use random grouping, introductions and a reason for each person to contribute, so that nobody sits outside the group's social life.

name: Compose a small group deliberately
description: put a group of three or four together on purpose: small enough that everyone has a job, without a single student of a particular background isolated in it, and with quieter students placed together so they get airtime instead of being talked over.

name: Classroom norm
description: Classroom norm: an expectation about how the room treats an idea - everyone here has something to learn, all ideas are treated respectfully. A rule governs conduct; a norm governs what happens to an answer.

name: State a norm and enforce it the first time it is tested
description: state the norms of the room early, and act the first time one is tested, because that is when the group finds out whether you meant it.

name: Plan a group session end to end
description: plan one session whole: a routine that opens it, a task worth doing together, questions chosen on purpose, a way of finding out whether it landed, and a close.

name: Closed and open questions
description:
Closed question: one with few right answers, asked to steer toward a particular answer or to check that something taught has stuck.
Open question: one with a range of valid answers, asked to make students think, connect several things at once, or tell you what they actually believe.

name: Place a question on the closed-open spectrum
description: decide where a question really sits, from what a student has to do to answer it - and catch that why and explain can just as easily be asking for something memorised.

name: Ask the kind of question you actually want answered
description: decide before asking whether you want to steer, to check, or to find out what the group thinks, and ask accordingly - including noticing when you are asking a closed question because you are afraid of losing the room.

name: Wait time I and II
description:
Wait time I: the pause between asking a question and doing anything else. Left alone it is about a second.
Wait time II: the pause after a student has answered, before you react.

name: Hold the pause for three to five seconds
description: wait after asking, and wait again after an answer, instead of rephrasing or answering it yourself - and say what the pause buys: longer answers, more volunteers, fewer flat failures to respond, and students comparing with each other instead of routing everything through you.

name: Think, Pair, Share
description: Think, Pair, Share: a question put to the room in three steps - each person thinks alone, then compares with the person next to them, then the pairs report back to the group.

name: Run a Think, Pair, Share
description: run the three steps with a real question, and drop one of them on purpose when the session calls for a TP, a PS or a TS instead.

name: Explain what each part of TPS contributes
description: say what Think, Pair and Share each do: retrieval and individual responsibility, a rehearsal that lowers the cost of being wrong, and what the rest of the room learns from hearing another pair.

name: Collect answers by asking what a pair talked about
description: ask what a pair talked about rather than putting the original question again, so that a pair who went somewhere else can say so without being caught out, and so the room hears what else was in play.

name: Steering group
description: Steering group: a few students spanning low, average and high prior attainment, picked in advance and not told, whose answers tell you whether an explanation landed.

name: Find out whether it landed without asking for questions
description: put a couple of questions to your steering group and read the result: if your strongest student cannot answer, reteach the whole group; if your average student cannot and your strongest can, reteach before moving on.

name: Manage who gets heard
description: run hands up and wait, ask for two or three hands before taking any answer, and ask openly for hands from those who have not had a turn, so that the same three students do not answer everything.

name: Call on people at random, and frame it so it is not a punishment
description: use sticks, cards or the class list to call on anyone, framed as everyone here having something worth hearing rather than as a penalty for not volunteering.

name: Rotate who reports back for a group
description: name a reporter for each small group and change who it is, by a rule harmless enough that nobody reads anything into it.

name: Run a whip-around
description: take a response under thirty seconds from every single person in the room, and judge when the group is small enough, and the term early enough, for it to be worth the minutes.

name: Keep track of who has not spoken
description: hold a running sense through a session of who has said something and who has not, and invite the ones you have not heard from.

name: Take an answer without judging it on the spot
description: acknowledge an answer neutrally and come back to it, rather than confirming or correcting immediately, so that half-formed and wrong ideas surface where you can do something about them.

name: Use praise carefully
description: say what heaping praise on one answer does to everyone else's willingness to add anything, and acknowledge simply instead.

name: Stop repeating student answers back to the room
description: let an answer stand, or ask for it again louder, instead of relaying it yourself, because relaying trains the room to listen to you rather than to each other.

name: Ask for the students' own questions
description: invite questions actively, rather than reading silence as there being none.

name: Keep what you ask and what you assess consistent
description: notice when you ask open questions in the session and then test only recall, and say what that quietly tells students actually counts.

name: Cognitive-memory, convergent, divergent and evaluative thinking
description:
Cognitive-memory thinking: recalling something already known.
Convergent thinking: narrowing several pieces toward the one correct answer.
Divergent thinking: generating several possible answers rather than one.
Evaluative thinking: judging something against a standard, and being able to say which standard.

name: Bloom's taxonomy
description: Bloom's taxonomy: six levels of educational objective - knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis and evaluation. Closed questions cluster at the knowledge end, open ones reach toward synthesis and evaluation.

name: Count what you actually asked
description: sort the questions you asked in one session by what they demanded, and hold the result against the finding that around 60 per cent of teachers' questions ask only for recall, 20 per cent for real thinking and 20 per cent are about procedure.

name: Answer-making and sense-making
description:
Answer-making: working on a question in order to produce an answer. Quick to mark, easy to reward, and nearly silent about whether anything is understood.
Sense-making: working on a question in order to understand it - connecting the parts into a whole, and recognising the problem as one instance of a more general relationship.

name: Shift a room from answer-making toward sense-making
description: explain why students arrive at university already expert at answer-making, and pick the task, question or device that makes understanding the thing that pays in your room.

name: Whiteboarding
description: Whiteboarding: three or four students at one large board, working out and defending a shared representation of a problem, so that the thinking sits between them instead of inside one head.

name: Explain what a whiteboard does that paper does not
description: account for the three: room for several representations side by side, erasing cheap enough that a half-formed idea can be tried out, and content the group has to agree on because any of them may be asked to defend it.

name: Small-group and whole-group discourse
description:
Small-group discourse: students rehearsing an idea at their own board, at far less risk of embarrassment, where you can circulate and listen before anything is final.
Whole-group discourse: the boards compared in front of everyone, where an idea has to survive the room.

name: Board meeting
description: Board meeting: the whole group sitting in a circle comparing boards, where your job is to keep asking how do you know, what if, and why did you choose that - until the students start asking it themselves.

name: Run a board meeting
description: hold a whole-group comparison of boards, prompt with how do you know, what if and why did you choose, and hand the questioning over to the students.

name: Norms for a good whiteboard
description:
Multiple representations: the same idea shown more than one way - a graph, a diagram, an equation.
Scaled and labelled: axes, quantities and units written on, at a scale that can be read from across the room.
Coordinated: every representation on the board telling the same story.

name: Judge a board against the norms
description: look at a group's board and say which of the three norms it meets and what would have to change.

name: Paradigm lab, practice-with-the-model and questionless problems
description:
Paradigm lab task: characterise the relationship between two measurable quantities.
Practice-with-the-model task: apply a model already built to a situation it has not been used on.
Questionless problem: a situation handed over with no question attached, where the group has to generate answerable questions of its own.

name: Choose a task worth putting on a board
description: pick or rewrite a task so that the board earns its place, using one of the three shapes rather than a question with a single number for an answer.

name: Get a group out of the algebra and back to the problem
description: notice when a group has zoomed in on symbolic detail and lost the model, and send them back to what the numbers stand for - a sketch before an equation.

name: The SOLO taxonomy
description:
Prestructural: the answer misses the point of the task, uses irrelevant material, or rests on a guess.
Unistructural: one relevant piece of the problem, taken literally.
Multistructural: several relevant pieces, listed but unconnected.
Relational: the pieces integrated into a whole, with the connections between them understood.
Extended abstract: the structure generalised beyond the problem given, to a situation it was not built for.

name: Place an answer on the SOLO taxonomy
description: listen to what a group says about a problem, say which level the answer is sitting at, and say what it would take to move it up one.

name: The two dimensions of feedback
description:
Positive and negative feedback: feedback aimed at what was done well, and feedback aimed at what was not. This is the dimension of tone.
Constructive and unconstructive feedback: feedback the recipient can act on, and feedback they cannot. This is the dimension of usefulness, and it is the one that decides whether the feedback was worth giving.

name: Give feedback the recipient can act on
description: say specifically what to keep doing on purpose, or what to do differently, whether the feedback is positive or negative - and catch yourself when great job or that was a bit unclear has left the other person nothing to act on.

name: Content, slides and style
description:
Content: what is to be communicated. Limited, relevant to this audience, and organised.
Slides: clear, simple, little text, big enough to read from the back.
Style: spoken clearly and at a pace people can follow, with visible interest in the subject and eye contact with the room.

name: Tell a presenter the two things that matter most
description: explain why being clear and looking up are worth more preparation than humour and animation, from what experienced reviewers actually comment on when they watch a talk.

name: Prepare a short talk against the do's and don'ts
description: plan a short presentation with a few clear points pitched at the audience's level, slides that are simple and readable, and a delivery that is slow, clear and finishes inside its time.

name: Give feedback on a presentation, sorted by domain
description: watch a presentation, sort what you noticed into content, slides and style, and give it back constructively rather than merely positively or negatively.

name: Pedagogical model
description: Pedagogical model: a simplified account of how teaching or learning works. All models are wrong and some are useful: the job of one is not to say what is right, but to give you words for what you are doing and why.

name: Working memory
description: Working memory: where thinking actually happens, right now. It holds about four things at a time, and it is easily overloaded.

name: Long-term memory
description: Long-term memory: where knowledge is stored, with no known limit on how much fits. It holds facts, procedures, beliefs and dispositions.

name: Schema
description: Schema: a chunk of related knowledge in long-term memory, bundled into one unit with a job to do - a schema for adding fractions, a schema for reading a graph.

name: Encoding
description: Encoding: storing something from working memory into long-term memory. This is what has happened when something has been learned.

name: Retrieval practice
description: Retrieval practice: pulling something back out of long-term memory into working memory. Retrieving a thing changes how easily it comes back next time, so a quiz is a way of teaching and not only a way of measuring.

name: Declarative and procedural learning
description:
Declarative learning: learning through working memory. Fast, and fragile.
Procedural learning: learning through repetition and constant feedback. Slow, and solid. Practice does not make perfect; it makes permanent.

name: Extraneous load
description: Extraneous load: the demand a session makes on working memory that has nothing to do with what is being learned - an unclear instruction, a routine nobody knows yet, five minutes spent working out what the task even is.

name: Automaticity
description: Automaticity: knowledge that comes back at no cost to working memory at all, built by long repetition. What is automatic is hard to dislodge, which is also why an automated bad habit is so expensive.

name: Surface and deep structure
description:
Surface structure: what a problem is dressed up as - the ages, the shopping trip, the train leaving a station.
Deep structure: the relationship the problem is actually an instance of, which an expert sees at once and a novice does not see at all.

name: The curse of knowledge
description: The curse of knowledge: once you know something well you can no longer reconstruct what it was like not to know it, so you systematically underestimate where a student gets stuck.

name: Memory is the residue of thought
description: Memory is the residue of thought: students remember whatever occupied their working memory, which is not necessarily what the session was about, and not necessarily what you meant them to think about.

name: A method that lasts
description: A method that lasts: one that still works when the problem changes shape. A shortcut that gets today's answer and collapses next topic leaves behind a schema that has to be unlearned before anything else can be built.

name: Explain why knowing a subject is not the same as teaching it
description: explain, in terms of automaticity and deep structure, what an expert does that a novice cannot, and name something in your own subject whose difficulty you can no longer see.

name: Predict what students will attend to
description: look at an activity you are planning and say what students will be thinking about while they do it, rather than what it is about, and change the activity when the two come apart.

name: Cut the load that is not about the thinking
description: find what in a session is spending working memory without teaching anything, and take it out.

name: Build retrieval into a session
description: plan a point in a session where students have to pull something out of memory rather than recognise it on a slide, and say why that counts as teaching.

name: Judge how long a method will last
description: ask of a method you are about to teach how long it will serve, how you would move students on from it, and whether it will have to be undone later - and teach the harder general method when the answer says so.

name: Justify a teaching choice with a model
description: account for a change you made to your own teaching using one of the models in this course, and say what that model does not capture.

name: Competence, autonomy and relatedness
description:
Competence: believing you are able to do the thing.
Autonomy: having a real choice in how you do it.
Relatedness: belonging in the room you are doing it in.

name: Diagnose a flat session with the three needs
description: when something is not working, ask which of competence, autonomy and relatedness is missing, and name what in the session would supply it.

name: Give the group a real choice
description: build a genuine choice into a session - which method to try, which question to take first, how the groups are put together - rather than the appearance of one.

name: Subject anxiety
description: Subject anxiety: anxiety about a subject, only weakly related to how able a student is. It occupies working memory that would otherwise go on the problem, so it costs most on demanding tasks and almost nothing on automated ones - and it can cost the students with the largest working memories the most, because they are the ones attempting the most ambitious strategies.

name: Act on a student's anxiety instead of validating it
description: use the four countermeasures: secure the fundamentals, watch what your own anxiety about a topic does to the room, think twice about timed work in both directions, and answer a struggling student with confidence and a concrete strategy rather than with not everyone is good at this.

name: Equitable teaching strategy
description: Equitable teaching strategy: a way of structuring who gets to think, talk and be taken seriously, so that access does not default to whoever is already most confident. It does not mean lowering the bar.

name: Explain why structure matters
description: argue, from the finding that feeling excluded measurably affects performance even in students who have succeeded at the subject before, why the way a room is structured is part of whether the content reaches everyone in it.
